item.title: Rod 002: 6'6" 1pc Light Spinning (French Broad)
item.description:
A one-piece split-cane spinning rod for winter fishing on the French Broad around Hap Simpson Park in Brevard, late November through December. It’s milled full-length on the Morgan Hand Mill’s extension bed. This is my first spinning rod, so the page also covers the spinning basics a fly-rod builder doesn’t already know: power classes, the reel seat, guides, the reel, and lures.

The spec in one line: 6'6", one piece, hex, light power / moderate-fast action, 4–6 lb line, lures 1/16–1/4 oz (designed around 1/8 oz), sliding-ring cork grip, a 1000-size reel.

Status: design only. The taper below hasn’t been cut yet. Check it in Hexrod before planing (see Taper).

The water: French Broad at Hap Simpson, Nov–Dec

  • Where: Hap Simpson Park is a City of Brevard river access with a boat ramp and picnic tables, at about mile 21.5 of the French Broad Paddle Trail. It’s the take-out for the flat, calm ~10-mile float down from Island Ford. The Pisgah Forest access is about 5 miles downstream.
  • What it’s like: The mainstem here is slow, sandy, deep-bend water, not freestone pocket water. In winter, fish hold in the deep slow pools, on the outside bends, and around woody cover. Expect holdover stocked trout and resident browns, plus smallmouth, redbreast sunfish and rock bass, all sluggish in cold water.
  • Regulations (verify before fishing): A third-party county guide lists the mainstem from the West/North Fork junction down to the US 276 bridge as Hatchery Supported trout water. That reach should include Hap Simpson, but I haven’t confirmed it against the NCWRC rule text. Under Hatchery Supported rules: 7 trout/day, no minimum length, and no bait or lure restrictions. You need an NC fishing license plus the trout privilege on designated public mountain trout waters.
  • Best fishing nearby in this window: The fresh fish are in the Delayed Harvest waters. These are the East Fork French Broad (NCWRC scheduled its fall 2026 stocking for Nov 10 after warm water cancelled October) and DuPont’s Little River. DH runs catch-and-release, artificial lures with one single hook only. Build the tackle box around single-hook lures and one kit covers both waters (see Tackle).
  • Stocking caveat: Bobby N. Setzer hatchery, right up the Davidson, closed in late 2025 for renovation, so NCWRC now stocks from Armstrong. Check the NCWRC stocking schedule instead of assuming past patterns.
  • Flows: USGS 03443000, French Broad at Blantyre is the closest mainstem gage below Brevard.

The Brevard / DuPont / Highlands dossier has the rest of the region: shops, the DH calendar, and Helene access notes.

Power class: ultralight vs. light

Spinning rods are rated by power (how much force it takes to bend the rod; roughly, the line and lure weights it handles) and action (where it bends: fast = mostly the tip, moderate = into the middle). This is the spinning equivalent of a fly rod’s line weight.

Class Line Lures Good for Here
Ultralight (UL) 2–4 lb 1/32–1/8 oz small creeks, small fish, short casts Fits the East Fork and creeks. Underpowered for the mainstem’s width, current, and the odd big brown or smallmouth.
Light (L) 4–6 lb 1/16–1/4 oz small rivers, stocked trout, bass Pick this. It casts across the mainstem pools, handles a 1/4 oz spoon or jerkbait, and is still fun on a 10" stocker.
Medium-light (ML) 6–8 lb 1/8–3/8 oz bigger rivers, bass-first fishing Overgunned for winter’s small, slow lures.

Light wins because this rod has to cover both the wide, slow mainstem and the small DH runs, and winter lures are small (1/16–1/8 oz) but sometimes need distance. A bamboo light rod still casts 1/16 oz well, because a cane rod’s own mass helps load it. Thomas & Thomas labeled their classic 5'6" spinner “ultralight,” and a builder who measured one rated it light-to-ultralight in the hand. That’s the feel I’m after here.

Rod spec

key value
geometry hex (6)
rod length 6 ft 6 in (78")
pieces 1 (no ferrule)
power / action light / moderate-fast
line 4–6 lb mono
lure weight 1/16–1/4 oz (design point 1/8 oz)
tip 0.080" → tiptop tube 6/64
butt (grip) 0.268–0.270"
handle 12" full cork, two sliding rings
guides 6 single-foot + tiptop (16 mm stripper)
strip length 89" (78 + 4 tip + 5 butt + 2 hold-down)

Building it one piece

The Morgan Hand Mill’s extension bed (a 36" bolt-on) handles one-piece rods up to about 7'6", so a 6'6" rod fits with a foot to spare and doesn’t need a splice. Per the manual notes:

  • Each strip is cut on both finishing anvils, switching once. The tip-to-butt anvil changeover lands between bed stations #7 and #8.
  • Mill-stop hole B for rough and finish butt; hole A for finish tip.
  • Strip length = rod + 4" tip + 5" butt + 2" hold-down = 89".

What changes compared with the 2-piece class build:

  • Culms. The class method cuts culms into 5–6’ sections. A one-piece needs ~7'6"+ of clean culm per strip. Take the strips from the lower 8’ of a 12’ culm so the butt gets the dense power fibers. Expect 5–6 nodes per strip. Keep the 3×3 stagger, and keep nodes out of the top 6" (tiptop) and out of the reel-ring area.
  • Heat treating is the real constraint. An 89" strip won’t fit a kitchen oven. Options, best first:
    1. A long tube oven: an 8’ steel or aluminum tube, heat gun, and a thermometer at each end. Flip the strips end for end halfway through, same as the forced-air note in the class sheet.
    2. Flame the culm before splitting. This is period-correct: Paul Young’s 1953 Spin-Caster was “medium flamed.”
    3. Splice. Scarf-join a butt strip and a tip strip with a long (3–4") bevel. Stagger the six splices so no two land within ~6" of each other, and keep them out of the top 30" where the rod flexes most. This triples the glue-line risk, so use it only if 1 and 2 are out.
  • Handling. A 7’+ strip whips around on the bench and in the binder. Support it on both ends while planing, and bind in one pass end to end.
  • Hanging to dry and storage. You need a clear 8’ vertical drop to hang the blank. A finished rod in a 6'10" tube rides diagonally in most cars.

Taper

No published taper matched the spec, so I designed this one from published bamboo spinning tapers on bamboorodmaking.com:

  • Richard Tyree’s 6’ (lures to 1/4 oz): the closest match, tip 0.079
  • the T&T Classic 5'6" (2–4 lb, to 1/4 oz): tip 0.072
  • Paul H. Young’s 6'4" Spin-Caster: tip 0.096, a heavier tip

My taper scales Tyree’s rod to 78" with a nearly straight taper (the method most of those builders describe: ~0.014–0.016" per 5" station) and a flat, slightly thickened butt under the grip. A tip at 0.080 follows Ian Kearney’s advice that a light open-face rod “needs to come down to closer to .075.”

Sanity check, not a substitute for Hexrod. I ran a rough static-stress comparison: a point lure load at the tip plus the cane’s own weight, stress = M / (0.1203·d³). At 1/8 oz this taper’s stress curve is flat from 15" to the grip and sits at the same level as Tyree’s proven 6’ rod, with a slightly protected tip.

  • At 1/4 oz the load moves toward the tip.
  • At 1/16 oz the rod’s own weight dominates and the butt does more of the work.

That’s the moderate-fast behavior I want, centered on 1/8 oz. Before cutting, run it through Hexrod (it models casting load and gives stress at each 5" station) and compare it against Tyree’s 6'.

Bed rise is the cumulative raise from the thickest station in each half, the same convention as Rod 001. The largest change between adjacent stations is 0.008", well under the bed’s 0.020" limit.

Handle and reel seat

The big difference from a fly rod is that the reel sits partway up the handle, not at the butt, and it hangs below the rod on a stem. Your casting hand wraps the seat with the reel stem between two fingers. The rear grip runs back along your forearm, and your index finger reaches the spool to feather the line. There’s no line hand: the reel does all the line handling.

Option A (recommended): full cork with sliding rings

The classic bamboo spinning handle (T&T, Paul Young, and the Montague-derived 6’ on bamboorodmaking all use it). It’s just a fly-rod cork grip with no seat hardware. The reel foot sits on the cork and two metal rings slide over its ends.

 tip butt
---------+-+------------+------+-------------+------+------------+---+
blank | | cork | ring | reel foot | ring | cork |cap|
---------+ | | | | | | |
+-+------------+------+----+---+----+------+------------+---+
winding | | stem
check .--+---+--.
| reel |
'---------'
|<-------------------------- 12" cork ------------------------>|
|<------- ~3.5" ---------->|<------------ ~8.5" --------------->|
66" from tip reel-foot center 78" butt
  • 12" Portuguese cork (78" − 12" = cork starts at 66"). Shape it as one long cigar or a straight full-wells with a slight swell under the reel.
  • Rings: 2 nickel-silver or aluminum sliding rings sized to the cork’s diameter at the reel position, about 7/8–1". Lap the reel foot on the cork first; the rings should press it down snugly, not just touch.
  • Reel position: about 8.5" from the butt end to the center of the reel foot, then fine-tune by balance and forearm length. Hold it the way you’d fish it: the butt end should just reach the inside of your forearm.
  • Tradeoff: the lightest, cleanest, and most period-correct option, but rings can creep when it’s cold and wet. The fix is a strip of electrical tape under the foot or a slight taper in the cork so the rings jam.

Option B: skeleton seat (modern, locks solid)

A graphite skeleton seat (Fuji and ALPS make spinning versions in 16–18 mm) with split fore and rear grips. It’s mounted on a built-up arbor over the hex (masking tape or cork rings shaped round, epoxied).

| | fore | hood reel hood | rear grip |cap|
---------+ | grip | [=== foot ===] nut| (cork/EVA) | |

| | stem
.--+--+--.
| reel |
'--------'
|<-- 2.5" -->|<----- 3.5" ----->|<------- 6.5" ------->|
  • Fixed hood on one end, threaded hood plus lock nut on the other. Either direction works. Pick whichever puts the threads where your fingers don’t sit.
  • Tradeoff: the reel never moves, but you’ll have to make an arbor and it looks modern on cane.

Fly vs. spin at a glance

Fly rod Spinning rod
Reel position at the butt, below the grip 8–9" up from the butt, mid-handle
Reel orientation hangs below hangs below on a stem
What carries the cast the line’s weight the lure’s weight
Line control line hand strips line index finger on the spool, then turn the handle
Guides small snakes, small stripper fewer, larger single-foot guides; big stripper ring
Handed-ness usually reel with the off hand same: cast right, crank left (most reels swap sides)

Guides and tiptop

Line comes off a spinning spool in big coils, so the first guide (the stripper) is large and sits high. The rest step down to choke the coils into a straight line. Use light single-foot guides to keep weight off the cane tip. A rule of thumb from the bamboorodmaking page is one guide per foot of rod, plus one.

Position (from tip) Ring size Notes
0" 6 mm ring, 6/64 tube across-corners at the tip ≈ 0.092", so 6/64 (0.094") fits
5" 6 mm
11" 6 mm
18" 7 mm
26" 8 mm
35.5" 10 mm
47" 16 mm, high frame stripper, about 22" ahead of the reel foot

These are starting positions. Tape the guides on, mount the reel, and run the line through. Then do a static load test: tie the line off and bend the rod to about 90°, then move guides until the line follows the blank’s curve without touching it. Then cast with tape before wrapping. Wrap with fine thread, same as a fly rod; spinning guides don’t need special wrapping.

Reel

You want a 1000-size spinning reel (Shimano 1000 / Daiwa LT 1000–2000) that’s light (≈5.5–6.5 oz) and holds ~100+ yd of 4–6 lb mono. A heavier reel will make a 6'6" cane rod feel butt-heavy.

  • Modern pick: Shimano Stradic FM 1000HG (SKU ST1000HGFM): ~185 g / 6.5 oz, 6.0:1 gear, 3 kg drag. It’s the trout standard: smooth, durable, and easy to get serviced. FM is the current generation (the earlier one was FL), and HG means “high gear.”
  • Co-pick: Daiwa Ballistic MQ LT 1000: 6.2 oz on Field & Stream’s 2026 test scale. It’s the equal of the Stradic, so buy whichever is cheaper when you’re ready.
  • Shop by spec, not by name: 5.5–6.5 oz, 1000 size, aluminum spool, a drag that’s smooth at low settings (you’ll be running about 2 lb), and a handle that swaps sides. Published weights vary by source and model year, so confirm on the maker’s spec sheet. If you can, mount the reel on a rod in a shop to feel the balance.
  • Period-correct on cane: a vintage Mitchell 308 ultralight (the 408 is its faster-geared sibling: blue, with a screw-in handle). Check which side the handle cranks on any one you buy, because the vintage models vary. Look for a serviced one, because drags and bail springs on 50-year-old reels are the weak point.

Spinning basics for a fly angler:

  • Spool it right. Line comes off the filler spool the same direction it goes onto the reel, or you’ll fight twist all day. Fill to about 1/8" below the spool lip.
  • Set the drag to about 1/3 of the line test. With 6 lb line, the drag should slip at a ~2 lb pull on a scale.
  • Casting: pin the line on your index finger, open the bail, cast, and lift your finger to release. Touch the spool rim to feather or stop the lure. Close the bail by hand, not with the crank; that’s what stops line twist and loops.
  • Spinners twist line. Run a small ball-bearing swivel 18" ahead of any inline spinner.

Tackle

Everything below is single-hook or easy to convert, so the same box works on Hatchery Supported water (anything goes) and on the East Fork DH (one single hook, no bait). For DH, swap trebles for single siwash hooks with split rings and pliers, and take the second hook off a jerkbait.

Line: 6 lb mono for the mainstem; 4 lb is optional on the small DH runs. Mono is better than braid in December, because braid holds water and ices in the guides on freezing mornings. A 3’ 6 lb fluorocarbon leader is optional in gin-clear water.

Lure Size How to fish it in winter DH-legal?
Marabou or hair jig (black/olive, white) 1/32–1/16 oz Dead-drift or swim slowly along the bottom of deep pools. The top pick for cold water. ✅ single hook
Trout Magnet–style micro plastic on a 1/64 oz head 1/64 oz Under a small float through the slow pools. Deadly on stockers. ✅
2" curly-tail grub / small Ned rig 1/16 oz head Hop it slowly for winter smallmouth on the mainstem’s deep bends. ✅
Inline spinner (Panther Martin, Mepps #0–1, Rooster Tail) 1/16–1/8 oz Retrieve slowly, just fast enough to turn the blade. Swap to a single hook for DH. 🔧 convert
Spoon (Kastmaster, Phoebe) 1/12–1/8 oz Count it down, then flutter it back slowly. Good for long casts across the mainstem. 🔧 convert
Small floating or suspending minnow (Rapala F3/F5, CD3) ~1/8 oz Twitch and pause. Big browns and smallmouth will hit it. 🔧 one single hook
Nightcrawler on #8 hook + split shot — Hatchery Supported water only (bait banned on DH) ❌

Terminal kit: small ball-bearing swivels, round split shot (BB–#4), 1/2" float, #8 and #10 single hooks, single siwash hooks for conversions, a split-ring tool, forceps, a rubber-mesh net, and a small Plano box.

How to fish it: fish 11 a.m.–3 p.m., when the water is warmest. Fish slow and deep, close to the bottom of the deepest slow pools and the outside bends. Do several casts per spot before moving. Browns are spawning or just finished, so stay off redds: the clean, light-colored gravel patches.

Build checklist

  1. Run the taper in Hexrod and compare it against Tyree’s 6’. Adjust before cutting.
  2. Map the 5" positions to extension-bed station numbers (TODO above).
  3. Solve heat treating for 89" strips: tube oven, flamed culm, or splice.
  4. Select 12’ culms, take strips from the lower 8’, and stagger nodes 3×3.
  5. Rough → heat-treat → finish (both anvils, switching once) → dry bind → glue.
  6. Shape the 12" cork; fit the reel foot and rings at about 8.5" from the butt.
  7. Tape the guides and do the static load test, then a casting test. Then wrap and finish.
  8. Buy the reel and line, then build the tackle box above.
  9. Before the first trip, confirm the Hap Simpson reach’s designation, the NCWRC stocking schedule, and USGS flows.

Sources

item.title: 3D-Printed Rodmaking Tools
item.description:
Small shop tools for the bamboo build process. The blank-making tools tie to steps of the Morgan Hand Mill workflow; the grip, ferrule, and finishing tools serve the later stages the class notes stop short of. All are FDM-printable in PETG or PLA, generated parametrically, and validated watertight. STLs export in print orientation.

Parametric source: generate_rod_tools_stls.py — edit the parameter block (indicator stem size, ferrule bore, PVC diameter) and re-run to fit your hardware.

Depth-gauge base

For: checking strip dimensions over steel planing forms — the “set taper from spreadsheet” and final-planing steps.

A 70 × 40 base that rides the flats of the planing form on two end pads (the middle is relieved so bamboo dust doesn’t tilt it). A 3/8"-stem dial indicator drops through the centre bore and a printed pinch slit with an M4 cross-bolt clamps it: the socket-head bolt drives through a deep access tunnel on one side, and the nut drops into a top-loaded hex track on the other. Fit a 60° contact point to the indicator and it reads strip depth in the form groove directly.

depth_gauge_base.stl · print 1 · hardware: M4 × 35 socket-head bolt + nut, dial indicator with 3/8" stem and 60° point

Node-sanding jig

For: “sand nodes on disc sander until flat & flush with enamel” — the fancy sanding jig the class notes tell you to use if you have one.

A 90 mm block with an 8.2 mm channel: the strip lies enamel-down with the node proud of the face, and the printed tapered wedge presses in alongside to friction-lock it — no hardware at all. Present the jig face to the disc sander and the node sands dead flush without dishing the strip on either side.

node_sanding_jig.stl + node_jig_wedge.stl · print 1 each · no hardware

Strip-sanding plate

For: flattening/leveling the enamel face along a strip’s full length — the hand-sanding counterpart to the node jig above.

A 250 mm plate with a 60° V-channel down its length. The strip drops in point-down on its beveled (pith-side) edge; the enamel face sits proud above the flat rails on either side. Run a flat sanding board over the top — once the board rides the rails flush, the enamel face is level for the whole length, and the rails stop you from sanding past it.

strip_sanding_plate.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Binding-cord spool caddy

For: cord payoff during binding — implements the Garrison article’s spool fix.

The bulk cord spool rides an M8 axle that drops into open cradle slots in the two uprights. The Ø3.5 socket in the base takes a 1/8" brass rod bent into an overhead loop: cord comes off the spool up through the loop, and the springy rod absorbs tension spikes instead of passing them into the wrap — the exact shock-absorber trick from the Garrison Binder article.

spool_caddy.stl · print 1 · hardware: M8 × 120 bolt (or M8 rod) + washers, ~300 mm of 1/8" brass rod, 4 wood screws

Cork press

For: gluing up a grip from cork rings.

Two Ø60 pressure discs and two six-lobed knobs with captive M8 nuts. Stack glued cork rings on a length of M8 threaded rod between the discs, spin the knobs down, and leave it to cure. Press the grip off-rod, then ream to the blank and glue it on.

cork_press_disc.stl ×2 · cork_press_knob.stl ×2 · hardware: M8 threaded rod ~300 mm

Finishing V-stands

For: supporting and hand-turning a blank during wrap finishing and varnish work.

120 mm-tall stands with a deep 90° V. Glue felt into the V so the blank turns without marking. Print two (or three for long butt sections) and screw them to a board at whatever spacing the section needs.

finishing_v_stand.stl ×2 · hardware: felt strip, 4 wood screws

Ferrule slitting collar

For: cutting even serrations in ferrule tangs.

A collar that slips over the ferrule with six 0.7 mm saw-guide slots. The slots stop 4 mm above the base, so the jeweler’s saw bottoms out at a consistent depth and the cuts land at exactly 60° spacing. The bore is parametric — regenerate for each ferrule size you use (the included STL is Ø7.0).

ferrule_slit_collar.stl · print per ferrule size · hardware: jeweler’s saw

Varnish dip-tube cap

For: dust-free drying after dip-varnishing in a 1.5" PVC tube.

Caps the tube; the Ø10 centre hole passes the hanging wire so the freshly dipped section can drip and dry inside, sealed from shop dust. It prints pocket-up with zero overhang — flip it over to fit the tube. Regenerate PVC_OD if your tube measures differently.

dip_cap.stl · print 1

Print settings

PETG or PLA, 0.2 mm layers, 3–4 perimeters, 30–40% infill. No supports on any part. The depth-gauge base benefits from a dead-flat first layer — print it alone on a clean bed.
